prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Los Alamos National Laboratory announced Wednesday it is notifying nearly 2,000 current and former employees and visitors that they may have been exposed to beryllium in the lab and may be at risk of disease. Officials are trying to determine the source of beryllium found at Los Alamos National Laboratory. "Letters went out to all of them today," said Kevin Roark, a spokesman for the New Mexico laboratory. Concern over possible exposure to the hard, gray metal, which is purified for use in nuclear weapons and reactors and also used in bicycle frames and golf clubs,  was first raised last November, when a box containing beryllium was received at the laboratory's short-term storage facility, he said. "The package appeared to have damage or degradation of the packing materials, which prompted us to test the area for additional contamination," he said. Surface contamination was found, but it turned out that the box was not the source, Roark said, adding that the source has not been determined. Since the contaminated area had not been tested for the presence of beryllium since 2001, everyone who has entered the restricted-access area since then is being alerted, he said. "It's just one building at one technical area," Roark said, noting that the laboratory covers 36 square miles and has nearly 10,000 employees. Beryllium is hazardous only when its fine, particulate form is inhaled, he said. It was found on surfaces, not in the air, he said.  Find out more about beryllium » . Roark said the alert was sent because "we think it's the responsible, prudent thing to do to let people know we discovered this contamination and to answer their questions if they have any concern about potential for exposure." There are no reports of sickness and "we don't expect anyone to be ill," he said. The laboratory said about 240 employees and 1,650 visitors were potentially at risk because they visited the contaminated areas. About 2 percent of the exposed employees could become sensitized, a smaller percentage of whom could develop chronic beryllium disease, Roark said. Inhalation of powdered beryllium can result in chronic beryllium disease, which can impair lung function in people who are susceptible. The risk to the visitors would be "extremely low" because of the activities they performed and their short exposure time, Roark said. An operator will be available at the laboratory at 505-665-7233 from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Mountain Time, Monday through Friday.

(CNN) — Los Alamos National Laboratory announced Wednesday that it is notifying nearly 2,000 current and former employees, as well as visitors, that they may have been exposed to beryllium at the laboratory and could be at risk of disease.

Officials are working to determine the source of beryllium found at Los Alamos National Laboratory.

“Letters went out to all of them today,” said Kevin Roark, a spokesman for the New Mexico laboratory.

Concerns about possible exposure to the hard, gray metal—which is purified for use in nuclear weapons and reactors and is also used in bicycle frames and golf clubs—were first raised last November, when a box containing beryllium was received at the laboratory’s short-term storage facility, Roark said.

“The package appeared to have damage or degradation of the packing materials, which prompted us to test the area for additional contamination,” he said.

Surface contamination was found, but the box ultimately was not the source, Roark said, adding that the source has not yet been determined.

Because the contaminated area had not been tested for the presence of beryllium since 2001, everyone who has entered the restricted-access area since then is being alerted, he said.

“It’s just one building at one technical area,” Roark said, noting that the laboratory spans 36 square miles and employs nearly 10,000 people.

Beryllium is hazardous only when inhaled in its fine particulate form, he said. It was found on surfaces, not in the air. Find out more about beryllium »

Roark said the alert was issued because “we think it’s the responsible, prudent thing to do to let people know we discovered this contamination and to answer their questions if they have any concern about potential for exposure.”

There have been no reports of illness, and “we don’t expect anyone to be ill,” he said.

The laboratory said about 240 employees and 1,650 visitors were potentially at risk because they had visited the contaminated areas.

About 2 percent of exposed employees could become sensitized, and a smaller percentage of those individuals could develop chronic beryllium disease, Roark said.

Inhalation of powdered beryllium can result in chronic beryllium disease, which can impair lung function in susceptible individuals.

The risk to visitors would be “extremely low” because of the activities they performed and the brevity of their exposure, Roark said.

An operator will be available at the laboratory at 505-665-7233 from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Mountain Time, Monday through Friday.

counterfactuals.output:
**Beryllium found on surfaces in restricted Los Alamos building; workers, visitors to be notified**

LOS ALAMOS, N.M. — Los Alamos National Laboratory is notifying hundreds of employees and more than a thousand visitors after beryllium was detected on surfaces inside a restricted-access building at the lab, raising questions about possible exposure to a metal that can cause a serious lung disease in some people.

Lab officials said the beryllium was discovered through industrial-hygiene sampling — commonly called “swipe” or surface sampling — in an area not open to the general public. The sampling found traces of beryllium on surfaces, prompting the lab to review who may have entered the building and to notify people who could have had contact with affected areas.

The notifications are being sent to about **240 employees** and **1,650 visitors** who had access to the building during the period under review. Officials said the notices do not mean those individuals became ill or were necessarily exposed at harmful levels. Rather, the notifications are intended to inform them of the finding, explain potential health risks and advise them about medical screening options if appropriate.

Beryllium is a lightweight, strong metal used in aerospace, defense, nuclear and high-technology applications. At nuclear weapons laboratories, it can be used in specialized components and research activities. In solid form, beryllium is not generally considered dangerous to touch, but dust, particles or residue containing beryllium can pose a health hazard if inhaled or, in some cases, spread through contaminated surfaces.

The primary long-term health concern is **chronic beryllium disease**, or CBD. CBD is an immune-system reaction that occurs in a small percentage of people who become sensitized to beryllium. Once sensitized, a person’s immune system can overreact to even tiny amounts of beryllium, causing inflammation and scarring in the lungs.

Symptoms of chronic beryllium disease can include persistent cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, chest pain, fever, night sweats and unexplained weight loss. The disease can develop months or years after exposure, and some people may have no symptoms at first. Diagnosis typically involves medical history, lung testing, imaging and a blood test known as the beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test, which can identify beryllium sensitization.

The lab said it is taking steps to evaluate the affected areas, determine how the contamination occurred and prevent further spread. Such steps can include additional sampling, restricting access, enhanced cleaning, reviewing ventilation and work controls, and assessing whether any workers need medical follow-up under federal beryllium safety rules.

The incident underscores the continuing challenge of controlling legacy and operational hazards at national laboratories where beryllium has been used for decades. While the discovery of surface contamination does not automatically indicate airborne exposure, officials said notifying potentially affected people is required to ensure transparency and allow individuals to seek information about possible health risks.
